posts.body:
🎁 Are FREE GitHub Swags & Goodies Available?

The answer is yes, swag is part of the Dev Days program — but it is NOT guaranteed for every attendee.

GitHub's official organizer FAQ says that limited quantities of swag are available for in-person events and are distributed on a first-come, first-served basis. The listed swag includes event stickers and small raffle-style swag kits containing GitHub and VS Code merchandise.

So if you're attending a Dev Days event, don't assume that simply registering guarantees a complete swag kit.

Availability depends on the specific event and available inventory.

💻 What Exactly Is GitHub Dev Days?

GitHub Dev Days 2026 is designed around hands-on learning with GitHub Copilot and AI-assisted development.

The official GitHub Dev Days repository describes the events as practical sessions where developers can explore real-world workflows with GitHub Copilot. Events typically run for around 2–3 hours and can include technical sessions, demonstrations and workshops.

The current Dev Days program focuses heavily on the GitHub Copilot app and agent-driven development.

You can learn how to:

🤖 Work with AI coding agents

💻 Use GitHub Copilot

📋 Pick up issues and tasks

🛠️ Ask agents to work on code

🔍 Review changes

🔀 Work with pull requests

🚀 Explore AI-assisted development workflows

The official Dev Days website currently describes the program as hands-on workshops designed to help developers master GitHub Copilot.

🎯 Who Can Attend?

Dev Days is designed for developers and technology enthusiasts, and individual events can welcome participants with different experience levels.

You don't necessarily need to be an advanced developer.

If you're a:

🎓 College student

👨‍💻 Software developer

🌱 Beginner programmer

🤖 AI enthusiast

☁️ Cloud/DevOps learner

🧑‍💻 Open-source contributor

💡 Technology enthusiast

you can check the requirements of an event near you.

For example, a Dev Days event in Tirupati, India stated that it was open to developers and students of all experience levels, with basic GitHub familiarity and the ability to read code being helpful.

🛠️ What Will You Learn?

The exact agenda depends on the local event, but Dev Days is centered around GitHub Copilot and AI-assisted development.

You may encounter topics such as:

🤖 GitHub Copilot

Learn how AI can assist with software development.

🧠 LLMs

Understand the basics of the large language models powering modern AI coding tools.

💻 AI-Assisted Coding

See how developers can use AI to work through coding tasks.

📋 Issue-Based Development

Learn how AI agents can work with issues and project tasks.

🔎 Code Review

Explore workflows for reviewing AI-generated or AI-assisted changes.

🔀 Pull Requests

Understand how AI-assisted development can fit into existing GitHub workflows.

🧪 Hands-On Labs

Many Dev Days events include practical activities where you actually use GitHub Copilot rather than simply watching a presentation.

🎁 What FREE Swag Can You Get?

According to GitHub's official Dev Days organizer information, the available swag can include:

🏷️ Event Stickers

GitHub Dev Days event stickers are part of the listed swag.

🎁 Swag Kits

Some events can receive small raffle-style swag kits containing GitHub and VS Code merchandise.

🎟️ Raffles

The official FAQ also mentions entry into a GitHub Copilot Pro+ raffle associated with the program.

However, there is an important difference between:

“Swag is available at the event”

and

“Every attendee gets swag.”

Those are not the same thing.

GitHub specifically states that quantities are limited and distribution is first-come, first-served.

⚠️ So, Will EVERYONE Get FREE Swag?

❌ No guarantee.

This is probably the most important thing to understand before attending.

The official information says:

Limited quantity → First come, first served

So even if an event has Dev Days swag, there may not be enough for everyone who registers or attends.

Your chances can therefore depend on:

Event size

Number of swag kits supplied

Arrival time

Local organizer's distribution process

Available inventory

That's why it's a good idea to register early and follow the specific event's instructions.

📍 How Do You Find a GitHub Dev Days Event?

GitHub maintains an official events page where Dev Days is listed as a community-led event series.

You can check:

GitHub Events — Dev Days

The official Dev Days repository also directs attendees to the event calendar to find events in different cities.

🇮🇳 What About India?

There have been GitHub Dev Days events in Indian cities as part of the 2026 program.

For example, an event in Tirupati included:

Git & GitHub fundamentals

LLM introduction

GitHub Copilot introduction

Practical Copilot workflows

A hands-on lab

Q&A

Networking

Stickers and swag

The listed event was free with registration required.

This shows that the exact experience can vary by city, so always check the individual event page.

📝 How to Register

The process is generally simple.

Step 1️⃣ — Find an Event

Visit the official GitHub events page or Dev Days event calendar.

Step 2️⃣ — Choose Your City

Look for a Dev Days event that fits your location and schedule.

Step 3️⃣ — Open the Registration Page

Local events may use platforms such as Luma for registration.

Step 4️⃣ — Register

Complete the registration form and provide the requested information.

Step 5️⃣ — Save Your Confirmation

Keep your registration confirmation or QR code ready for event check-in.

Step 6️⃣ — Arrive Early

If you're interested in swag, arriving early can be particularly important because GitHub says quantities are limited and distributed first-come, first-served.

🔥 Why Should You Attend?

Don't attend only for the T-shirt or stickers.

The bigger value is the hands-on experience with GitHub Copilot and modern AI-assisted development.

You can potentially:

Learn → Build → Network → Experiment → Add Skills to Your Resume

For students, it can also be a great opportunity to meet other developers and community members.

For working developers, it can provide a practical introduction to newer AI-assisted workflows.

🤖 GitHub Copilot Is the Main Focus

One of the major themes of Dev Days 2026 is the evolution of software development through AI agents.

The current Dev Days workshop material focuses on the GitHub Copilot app, where developers can direct AI agents to work on issues, review changes and help move tasks through the development workflow.

This makes Dev Days particularly relevant if you're trying to understand how AI is changing the way developers write, review and maintain software.

⚠️ Don't Follow Old Dev Days Information

GitHub's Dev Days program has had different rounds and formats.

The earlier 2026 Dev Days round ran from March 15 to May 15, while the current GitHub dev-days repository describes the later global series as running from September 1 through October 31, 2026.

So if you find an older article or YouTube video talking about Dev Days registration, swag or dates, check whether it's referring to the current September–October 2026 series.

🎁 FREE SWAG: What You Should Remember

Let's make it extremely simple:

✅ Dev Days can have GitHub swag

Yes.

✅ Stickers are listed as event swag

Yes.

✅ GitHub/VS Code swag kits can be available

Yes.

⚠️ Does every attendee automatically get one?

No.

⚠️ Is swag unlimited?

No.

📦 How is it distributed?

GitHub says limited quantities are distributed first-come, first-served.

So don't register expecting a guaranteed backpack, T-shirt or complete goodie box.

🚀 Final Thoughts

GitHub Dev Days 2026 is much more than a swag event.

It's a community-led opportunity to learn about GitHub Copilot, AI-assisted coding, AI agents and modern developer workflows through practical sessions and workshops.

And yes, FREE GitHub and VS Code swag can be available, but the supply is limited and distribution is first-come, first-served.

So if you find a Dev Days event near you:

Register → Check the agenda → Prepare your GitHub account → Attend early → Participate in the workshop → Network → And, if available, grab your swag! 🎁🔥

Most importantly, don't go just for the goodies.

Go to learn something that can actually improve the way you build software.

posts.title: Understanding Cloud IAM
posts.summary: A practical beginner-friendly guide to understanding cloud iam, with key concepts, a learning workflow, common mistakes, and next steps.
posts.body:
## The idea in plain English

Understanding Cloud IAM is easier to understand when you connect the concept to a real problem. In software development, the goal is not to learn a tool because it is popular; it is to understand what it solves, what trade-offs it introduces, and when a simpler option is enough.

This guide introduces the core idea, the vocabulary you will encounter, and a practical way to begin. Treat the examples as learning patterns and check the official documentation for version-specific behavior before using them in production.

## Why it matters

Developers work with systems made of smaller components. A clear mental model helps you decide where a component belongs, how it communicates with the rest of the application, and how to debug it when something fails. It also helps you explain your design choices during code reviews and interviews.

For a beginner, focus on three questions:

- **Problem:** What pain point does this approach address?
- **Mechanism:** What happens step by step when it runs?
- **Trade-off:** What extra complexity, cost, or maintenance does it add?

## A practical learning workflow

1. Start with a tiny example that demonstrates one concept.
2. Run it locally and observe the output rather than copying code blindly.
3. Change one input or configuration value and predict what will happen.
4. Add error handling and test an invalid input.
5. Write down what you learned and the limits of the example.

For example, when exploring understanding cloud iam, create a small project with one responsibility. Keep configuration explicit, use meaningful names, and add a short README explaining how to run it. Small experiments make errors easier to understand than a large project assembled all at once.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Choosing a tool before defining the problem.
- Copying snippets without checking their assumptions or version.
- Ignoring security, performance, accessibility, or failure cases.
- Treating a tutorial as proof that a solution is production-ready.
- Skipping documentation and tests.

## What to learn next

After you understand the basics, build a small end-to-end project and document the decisions you made. Compare at least one alternative, test edge cases, and consult the official documentation for the framework or platform you use. That process builds durable skill—not just familiarity with terminology.

## Further reading

Start with the official documentation for the relevant language, framework, or platform. Prefer primary documentation and maintained standards over undated social posts. This article is an evergreen learning guide, not a report of a newly announced product release.

*Written for the B Tecky developer-learning community.*

posts.summary: Choose a contribution that fits your skills and follow the project’s process before writing code.
posts.body:
Choose a contribution that fits your skills and follow the project’s process before writing code.

## The core idea

A good first contribution may be documentation, a reproducible bug report, a test, or a small fix. The project’s contribution guide and recent activity are stronger signals than a label alone.

## A practical way to approach it

Read the README, contribution guide, code of conduct, and issue discussion. Reproduce the problem locally, ask focused questions when needed, make a small change, add a test if appropriate, and describe what you verified.

## Try it in a small project

Improve one confusing setup instruction and test it from a clean checkout. Include the exact command and expected output so maintainers can review the change quickly.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Do not open many duplicate issues or claim work before understanding the project. Be patient with review and respect maintainer decisions.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.

---
## Find a project that matches your interests

A good first contribution is not necessarily the issue labelled “good first issue.” Look for a project you understand or want to learn, with recent activity, clear documentation, and maintainers who explain how contributions are reviewed. A small documentation fix, test, or reproducible bug report can be a valuable first contribution.

Before writing code, read the README, contribution guide, code of conduct, license, and issue discussion. Check whether the issue is still open and whether someone is already working on it. If the problem is unclear, ask one focused question and explain what you have tried.

## Reproduce the problem first

Follow the documented setup from a clean checkout where possible. Record the exact command, expected behaviour, actual behaviour, and relevant environment details. A minimal reproduction helps maintainers confirm the issue and prevents you from solving a symptom that cannot be repeated.

For a bug fix, add a regression test that fails before the change and passes afterward. For documentation, test the instructions as a new contributor would. Keep the change focused so reviewers can understand it quickly.

## Work respectfully with maintainers

Do not claim an issue without following the project's process. Avoid posting repeated “any update?” comments or opening duplicate issues. Maintainers may be volunteers with limited time. Respond to review feedback constructively and explain any disagreement with evidence.

Use a descriptive branch and commit message. In the pull request, state the problem, the approach, and the checks you ran. If the change is incomplete, say so rather than implying it is ready.

## Build a contribution habit

Start with one small contribution and learn the project's workflow. After it is merged, review the feedback and look for a related improvement. Keep a record of what you learned and link to the public pull request in your portfolio only if the project permits it and the work is genuinely yours.

Do not copy code from another project without checking its license. Open source means the license grants specific permissions and conditions; it does not mean code is free of obligations.

**Further reading:** [GitHub: Contributing to projects](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/exploring-projects-on-github/contributing-to-a-project) and [Choose an open source license](https://choosealicense.com/).

posts.body:
🤖 What Is Google Gemini at Work?

Google Gemini is Google's AI assistant designed to help people with everyday tasks such as writing, brainstorming, research, summarization, analysis, content creation and productivity.

For businesses and organizations, Gemini is integrated into Google Workspace so that AI assistance can appear directly inside familiar applications.

For example, Gemini can help you:

✉️ Draft and improve emails in Gmail

📝 Write and refine documents in Google Docs

📊 Analyze information in Google Sheets

📽️ Create and work with presentations in Google Slides

🎥 Create content with Google Vids

🤝 Take meeting notes with Gemini in Google Meet

💡 Brainstorm ideas using the Gemini app

🔎 Research and summarize information

⚙️ Automate certain repetitive workflows

Google's Workspace Learning Center specifically lists Gemini assistance across Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Meet, Vids and Google Workspace Studio.

💰 Is Google Gemini at Work FREE?

This is the BIG question.

The answer is: It depends.

There isn't one universal rule saying that everyone gets the full Gemini at Work experience for free.

Google currently provides different levels of access depending on whether you're using:

Personal Google Account

Work Google Account

School Google Account

Google Workspace subscription

Workspace edition / AI add-on

For example, Google says some Gemini web-app features can be used without signing in, while additional features require a Google Account. Work accounts need a qualifying Workspace edition, and school accounts depend on whether the service has been enabled by the institution's administrator.

So don't confuse free access to some Gemini capabilities with full premium AI features inside Google Workspace.

👨‍💻 Can You Use Gemini With a Work Account?

Yes, but your organization controls much of the access.

Google's documentation states that most users with a work or school Google Account have access to Gemini Apps, but feature availability and data handling depend on the Workspace license.

This means your company may provide Gemini access, but you might not have exactly the same limits or features as someone using another Workspace edition.

Your administrator may also control which services are enabled.

So if you are using your company's Gmail account and don't see a particular Gemini feature, it doesn't necessarily mean that Gemini is unavailable.

Your organization may simply have a different license or administrator configuration.

🏢 Gemini Inside Google Workspace

This is where things become really interesting.

Google has integrated Gemini into the applications people already use at work.

✉️ Gmail

Gemini can help you draft emails, summarize conversations and find important information.

📝 Google Docs

You can use AI assistance to brainstorm, write, refine and organize content.

📊 Google Sheets

Gemini can help analyze information and work with data.

📽️ Google Slides

AI can assist with creating presentations and visual content.

🎥 Google Vids

Gemini-powered features can help with video creation.

🤝 Google Meet

Gemini can help with meeting-related tasks, including taking notes.

⚙️ Google Workspace Studio

Google also provides tools for creating AI-powered workflows that can automate everyday tasks.

Google describes these capabilities as part of its broader Workspace AI experience.

🆓 What Can You Get Without Paying?

If you're simply interested in trying Gemini, you don't necessarily need to immediately purchase a Workspace subscription.

Google's Gemini Apps documentation says that some features can be accessed without signing in, while signing in unlocks additional functionality and the ability to save activity.

For people who want to experiment with AI, this means you can start by exploring the Gemini experience before deciding whether you actually need a paid plan.

However, the exact limits and available features can change, so always check Google's current pricing and product pages before subscribing.

🏢 What About Google Workspace's Free Trial?

If you're interested in trying Google Workspace itself, Google currently provides a 14-day free trial for new Workspace subscriptions.

Google states that the trial allows up to 10 users to explore Workspace features. A payment method is required during setup, but Google says it isn't charged until the trial ends.

There is an important India-specific detail too.

Google says that if you use NetBanking in India as the primary payment method, you may need to make a prepayment during setup to verify the account; that amount is applied as credit.

So if you're planning to test Workspace through the free trial, read the billing information carefully before starting.

🚀 What Is Premium AI in Google Workspace?

Google's current Workspace offering includes Gemini and Gemini Notebook in its paid Workspace plans.

Google's India Workspace page currently describes AI capabilities such as:

Gemini app

Gemini Notebook

Gemini inside Gmail

Gemini inside Docs

Gemini inside Sheets

Gemini inside Meet

Google Vids

Google Workspace Studio

Google also states that business data remains confidential and isn't used to train models or for advertising in its Workspace AI offering.

The exact AI capabilities and usage limits vary between Workspace editions.

📊 What About AI Expanded Access?

For organizations that need higher AI usage limits, Google also offers AI Expanded Access as an add-on.

According to Google's current documentation, AI Expanded Access is available for:

Business Standard

Business Plus

Enterprise Standard

Enterprise Plus

It provides higher access to certain advanced AI capabilities across Workspace applications.

For example, Google's current documentation lists higher limits for features involving Docs, Drive, Sheets, Slides, Vids and other Workspace services.

This is primarily relevant to organizations that need substantially more AI usage rather than someone simply experimenting with Gemini.

🎓 What About Students?

If you're a student, your situation can be different.

Google says school Google Accounts can access Gemini when the service is enabled by the institution's administrator.

So if your college provides Google Workspace for Education, check whether Gemini has been enabled for your account.

Don't assume that having a college Gmail account automatically gives you every Gemini feature.

Your institution's administrator and the applicable Workspace license determine availability.

💼 Why Is Gemini Useful at Work?

The biggest advantage isn't simply “having an AI chatbot.”

The interesting part is having AI inside the applications you're already using.

Imagine starting your workday with dozens of emails.

Instead of manually reading every thread, AI can help summarize important information.

Then you need to create a report.

Gemini can help you brainstorm and draft content.

You have a spreadsheet full of data.

AI can help you analyze and understand it.

You have a meeting.

Gemini can assist with meeting notes.

And when you're preparing a presentation, AI can help you create and organize content.

This is the broader idea behind Gemini at Work: bringing AI assistance into everyday workflows.

⚠️ But Don't Trust AI Blindly

Google itself warns that Gemini can make mistakes.

AI-generated information should be reviewed, particularly when dealing with important business information or professional decisions. Google's Workspace learning materials explicitly warn that Gemini features may suggest inaccurate or inappropriate information.

So use Gemini as an assistant, not as an unquestioned source of truth.

Always review:

Important emails

Business reports

Numbers

Customer information

Code

Legal or financial content

Sensitive information

before using AI-generated output.

🔐 What About Company Data?

Data privacy is especially important when using AI at work.

Google's Workspace documentation describes Gemini as having enterprise-grade security and privacy, and its Workspace AI offering says company data isn't used to train models or for advertising.

However, employees should still follow their organization's policies.

Never paste confidential company information into an AI tool unless your organization permits it.

Your company's security policy should always take priority.

🧑‍💻 How Can You Start Using Gemini at Work?

Here's a simple A-to-Z approach.

1️⃣ Check Your Account

Determine whether you're using:

Personal Google Account

Work account

School account

2️⃣ Check Your Workspace Plan

If you're using a company account, your available Gemini features depend on your organization's Workspace license.

3️⃣ Open Gemini

Try the Gemini web experience and see which features are available to your account.

4️⃣ Start With Simple Tasks

Don't immediately try complicated workflows.

Start with:

Email → Summarization → Brainstorming → Writing → Research → Analysis

5️⃣ Learn Better Prompting

Instead of writing:

“Write an email.”

Try:

“Write a professional but friendly email to my manager explaining that the project deadline needs to be moved by two days. Keep it under 120 words.”

Better context generally produces more useful results.

6️⃣ Explore Workspace Integration

Once you're comfortable with the standalone Gemini experience, explore how Gemini works inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Meet and other Workspace applications.

🎯 Is Gemini at Work Worth Learning in 2026?

If you already use Google Workspace regularly, understanding Gemini can be extremely useful.

You don't need to become an AI engineer.

You simply need to understand:

What Gemini can do → Where it can help → How to prompt it → How to verify the output → How to use it responsibly

That's enough to start improving everyday productivity.

🔥 The Most Important Thing to Remember

Don't believe every post saying:

“Google Gemini at Work is completely FREE for everyone!”

That's an oversimplification.

Some Gemini capabilities are available without paying, while more advanced Workspace features depend on your account, subscription, administrator settings and applicable usage limits.

So before subscribing or assuming you have access to a particular feature, check Google's current official documentation and the Workspace plan associated with your account.

🔗 Official Google Resources

🤖 Gemini Apps

Google Gemini Help & Access

🏢 Google Workspace with Gemini

Google Workspace AI for Business

📚 Gemini API / AI Developer Resources

Google AI for Developers

🎓 Google Workspace AI Training

Google Workspace Generative AI Training

🚀 Final Thoughts

Google Gemini at Work 2026 isn't just another AI chatbot.

Google is integrating AI directly into the tools people already use every day — Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Meet, Vids and more.

And while some Gemini functionality is available without paying, full Workspace AI access isn't universally free. Your available features can depend on your Google account, Workspace edition, organization and administrator settings.

If you're a student, developer, employee, freelancer or business owner, it's worth spending some time learning how Gemini fits into your daily workflow.

Because in 2026, the important question isn't just:

“Do I know AI?”

It's:

“Do I know how to use AI effectively in my everyday work?” 🚀🤖

posts.title: Git Branching and Pull Requests for Solo Developers
posts.summary: Use branches and small pull requests to review your own changes and make rollbacks easier.
posts.body:
Use branches and small pull requests to review your own changes and make rollbacks easier.

## The core idea

A branch lets you isolate a change from the main line. A pull request provides a review point for diffs, tests, and discussion even when you are the only developer. Small changes are easier to understand and revert.

## A practical way to approach it

Create a branch for one task, commit focused changes with descriptive messages, open a pull request, run checks, and merge after reviewing the diff. Delete the branch after merging if it is no longer needed.

## Try it in a small project

For a homepage redesign, separate content changes from a backend migration. Preview each change and test the pages it touches before merging.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Do not commit secrets or generated build clutter. Avoid rewriting shared history on a branch other people are using.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.

---
## Why branches help even when you work alone

A branch isolates one task from the main line of development. It lets you experiment, review a focused diff, and keep unfinished work away from the version that should remain stable. A pull request is useful even for a solo developer because it creates a checkpoint for changes, tests, preview deployments, and a written explanation of intent.

Keep one branch focused on one logical outcome. A homepage redesign, a database migration, and a content update should not be mixed into one large change unless they truly depend on one another. Smaller changes are easier to review and roll back.

## A practical workflow

1. Start from an up-to-date main branch.
2. Create a descriptive feature branch.
3. Make small commits with clear messages.
4. Run relevant tests and inspect the diff.
5. Open a pull request that explains the purpose and risk.
6. Review the preview and checks before merging.
7. Confirm the production deployment and keep a rollback path.

A good pull request description answers what changed, why it changed, how it was tested, and what reviewers should pay attention to. Screenshots or preview links help for visual changes.

## Protect the main branch

Use automated checks for builds, tests, formatting, and other important validations. Keep secrets out of commits and use environment variables or a secret manager. Avoid force-pushing shared branches unless you understand who depends on them.

If a change causes a production problem, revert the merge commit or use the platform's documented rollback process. Do not make an unrelated emergency edit on top of an uncertain deployment without first understanding the current state.

## Review your own work deliberately

Read the full diff as if someone else submitted it. Look for accidental file changes, generated output, debug code, broken links, accessibility regressions, and missing tests. Visit the preview on desktop and mobile. A successful build proves that the project compiled; it does not prove that every user flow works.

For practice, make a small content or style change on a branch, open a pull request, and compare the branch preview with production before merging.

**Further reading:** [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow) and [About pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests).

posts.summary: If you've been hearing about Hacktoberfest 2026 and wondering how to register, what you need to do, and whether you can actually get FREE swag, you're in the right place.  Hacktoberfest 2026 is a little different from previous years. The event is running throughout October 2026, and this year the focus is on learning a
posts.body:
🎃 What Is Hacktoberfest 2026?

Hacktoberfest is a month-long celebration of open source that brings developers, students, creators and technology communities together.

For 2026, the event is centered around open-source AI and open-weight models, with activities available both online and in person. Anyone can participate, whether you're just starting your development journey or already have experience building software.

You can participate through:

💻 Online activities

🤖 Open-source AI challenges

🎥 Livestreams

🏆 DEV Challenges

🌎 Global Hack Week

🏙️ Local Hacktoberfest Fests

🛠️ Hack Days and Meetups

And yes, there are rewards and swag opportunities along the way.

📝 How To Register for Hacktoberfest 2026

The registration process is quite simple.

Step 1️⃣ — Go to Hacktoberfest

Start with the official website:

https://hacktoberfest.com/

Avoid registering through random websites or links promising guaranteed swag.

Step 2️⃣ — Sign In With MyMLH

Hacktoberfest 2026 uses MyMLH for participant registration.

According to the official Hacktoberfest website, signing in with your MyMLH account is the first step. It is free and takes only a short time.

Once you sign in, your Hacktoberfest participant dashboard becomes your central place for tracking activities and rewards.

Step 3️⃣ — Add Your Postal Address

This step is very important if you want to receive the physical sticker pack.

Hacktoberfest gives you two stickers simply for:

1. Signing in with MyMLH

2. Adding your postal address

You then need to complete at least one additional eligible activity to unlock the first physical sticker pack.

So don't just register and forget about your account.

🎁 How Do You Get FREE Swag?

This is probably the biggest reason many people are interested in Hacktoberfest.

The 2026 reward system works through virtual stickers and milestones.

The official online participation page says that you start with two stickers:

🎟️ Sign in
🎟️ Add your address

Then you can earn additional stickers through activities.

Once you collect three virtual stickers, a physical sticker pack is sent to you.

That means:

2 stickers = Sign-up + Address

+1 sticker = Complete an eligible activity

🎁 3 stickers = Physical sticker pack

🔥 What Activities Can Earn Stickers?

There are multiple ways to earn virtual stickers during Hacktoberfest 2026.

🎥 Livestreams

You can attend Hacktoberfest livestreams and check in using the code shown during the session.

There are milestones for attending:

1 livestream

3 livestreams

5 livestreams

Hacktoberfest launch livestream

Each eligible activity can contribute a sticker to your sticker book.

🏆 DEV Challenges

Another way to participate is through DEV Challenges.

Hacktoberfest has a launch-weekend challenge followed by four weekly open-source AI rounds.

The current schedule includes:

Launch Weekend: October 2–4

Week 1: October 5–11

Week 2: October 12–18

Week 3: October 19–25

Week 4: October 26–31

You'll need a DEV account to enter these challenges.

Connecting your DEV account to MyMLH is optional, but Hacktoberfest recommends doing it because it allows you to earn credit for DEV Challenge participation and receive a special DEV badge.

🌎 Global Hack Week

You can also participate in Global Hack Week: Hacktoberfest.

There are multiple sticker milestones associated with Global Hack Week, including:

Completing registration challenges

Checking into a livestream

Earning 15 points

Earning 30 points

Earning 75 points

So even if you're not comfortable contributing to an open-source repository, you have several ways to participate.

🏙️ What If I Want To Attend a Hacktoberfest Event?

You can also participate in person.

There are 300+ Fests happening around the world.

A Fest can be either a Hack Day or a Meetup.

🛠️ Hack Day

A Hack Day is essentially a mini hackathon.

You can build a project using open-weight models and/or open-source AI tools and present your project at the end.

There can also be prizes for winning projects.

🤝 Meetup

A Meetup is more focused on community interaction and learning.

It may include:

Technical talks

Workshops

Panels

Discussions

Networking

You don't necessarily need to build a project to attend a Meetup.

🎁 What About FREE T-Shirts and Swag?

Here's where you need to be careful.

Hacktoberfest does have physical swag, but T-shirts and event swag are available while supplies last.

They are not guaranteed for every participant, and the local Fest host decides how the swag is distributed. T-shirts are also not promised to online participants.

So don't believe posts saying:

“Just register online and you'll definitely get a Hacktoberfest T-shirt.”

That's not how the 2026 system works.

However, the online sticker pack is a separate reward that can be earned by completing the required activities.

⭐ How To Get Even More Rewards

If you want to go beyond the first sticker pack, there are additional milestones.

🎟️ 3 Stickers

Unlock the physical sticker pack.

✨ 10 Stickers

Earn a bonus holographic sticker in your mailed sticker pack.

🏆 17 Stickers

Become a Hacktoberfest Completionist.

Completionists are automatically entered into a raffle for a Hacktoberfest 2026 T-shirt or Arduino Uno Q board.

The current online page lists 24 stickers that can be collected across the available activities.

⚠️ Do Pull Requests Still Count?

This is probably the most important change if you've participated in Hacktoberfest before.

❌ No.

Pull requests and merge requests no longer count toward Hacktoberfest rewards in 2026.

The organizers say the change is intended to reduce low-effort or spam contributions that can create additional work for open-source maintainers.

That doesn't mean open-source contributions are banned.

You can absolutely continue contributing to open-source projects during Hacktoberfest.

They simply aren't being used as the reward mechanism this year.

👨‍💻 I'm a Beginner. Can I Participate?

Absolutely.

Hacktoberfest explicitly welcomes beginners.

You don't need to be an expert in AI, GitHub or open source before joining.

You can start by:

Creating your MyMLH account

Adding your address

Checking the activities page

Watching a livestream

Joining Global Hack Week

Exploring DEV Challenges

Finding a local Fest

Learning about open-source AI

The goal is to learn and build, not simply collect rewards.

📅 How Long Do You Have?

Hacktoberfest takes place throughout October 2026.

The online schedule includes livestreams, challenges and Global Hack Week activities throughout the month.

If you're interested, don't wait until the final day.

Some activities happen only at specific times, and certain Fests can have limited capacity or limited swag.

🚨 Important Things To Remember

Before you start, remember these points:

✅ Hacktoberfest 2026 is free

Online participation is free, and almost all Fests are free to attend.

✅ MyMLH registration is required

Sign in to create your participant profile.

✅ Add your postal address

You'll need it for physical rewards.

✅ Pull requests don't count toward rewards

Don't follow outdated Hacktoberfest tutorials that tell you to complete a specific number of PRs.

✅ Swag isn't universally guaranteed

In-person T-shirts and event swag are limited and distributed by local hosts.

✅ Sticker packs can be earned online

posts.title: Git Merge vs Rebase: A Practical Explanation
posts.summary: Understand how merging preserves branch history and rebasing replays commits onto a new base.
posts.body:
Understand how merging preserves branch history and rebasing replays commits onto a new base.

## The core idea

A merge combines histories and can create a merge commit. A rebase rewrites the commits in one branch so they appear on top of another base. Both can be useful; team conventions and the state of shared history matter.

## A practical way to approach it

Use merge when preserving the exact branch relationship is important. Rebase a private feature branch to update it before review if that matches your team’s workflow. Resolve conflicts carefully and run tests after either operation.

## Try it in a small project

Create two branches that change different lines, then merge them. Repeat with a rebase and inspect the log to compare the resulting histories.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Do not rebase commits that teammates are already building on unless everyone agrees. Rewriting shared history can create confusing duplicate commits.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.

---
## Two ways to integrate branch work

A merge combines the histories of two branches. It can create a merge commit that records how the histories came together, preserving the fact that work happened on a separate branch. A rebase takes commits from one branch and replays them on top of another base, creating new commit IDs and a more linear history.

Neither approach is universally better. Teams choose based on their history policy, review workflow, and whether a branch is shared. The most important rule is to avoid rewriting history that other people are already using without coordination.

## When a merge is useful

Merge is a straightforward choice when you want to preserve branch topology and integrate reviewed work without rewriting its commits. It is often appropriate for a shared feature branch or when the team wants the pull request to remain visible in the repository history. A squash merge is a different integration option that combines the pull request's changes into one commit on the target branch.

## When a rebase is useful

Rebase can update a private feature branch with the latest base branch and keep the resulting history linear. Because rebase rewrites commits, the branch's commit IDs change. If the branch has already been pushed, updating it may require a force push. Use the safer `--force-with-lease` option rather than a blind force push, and only when the branch ownership and team process make it appropriate.

## Resolve conflicts carefully

A conflict means Git cannot automatically combine overlapping changes. Inspect both versions and understand the intended behaviour before editing the conflict markers. After resolving, run tests and inspect the resulting diff. A successful rebase or merge command does not prove the application still behaves correctly.

## Try both in a disposable repository

Create a base branch and two feature branches that change different parts of a file. Integrate one using merge and another using rebase, then inspect `git log --graph --oneline --all`. Repeat with conflicting edits and practise resolving them. Use a temporary repository so experimentation cannot damage real work.

**Further reading:** [Git: Merge](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge) and [Git: Rebase](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase).

posts.title: Cybersecurity for Beginners: Threat Modeling a Web App
posts.summary: Map assets, entry points, trust boundaries, and likely threats before choosing security controls.
posts.body:
Map assets, entry points, trust boundaries, and likely threats before choosing security controls.

## The core idea

Threat modelling is a structured way to ask what can go wrong and which protections matter most. It starts with the application and its data, not with buying a tool or adding a long checklist.

## A practical way to approach it

Draw the user, browser, API, database, and third-party services. Identify sensitive assets, trust boundaries, and actions an attacker might attempt. Prioritize mitigations by likelihood and impact, then revisit the model when architecture changes.

## Try it in a small project

For a blog editor, consider account takeover, unauthorized publishing, malicious input, leaked API tokens, and denial of service. Map a concrete control to each meaningful threat.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Threat models are not one-time paperwork. Keep them proportional, validate controls with tests, and include abuse cases as well as accidental failures.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.

---
## Start with assets and trust boundaries

Threat modelling is a structured way to identify what an application must protect, where data moves, and how an attacker might misuse the system. Begin by listing assets such as user accounts, personal information, payment records, API credentials, and administrative actions. Then draw the main components: browser, application server, database, file storage, identity provider, and external services.

A trust boundary is a point where data or control crosses between components with different levels of trust. User input crossing into an API is one boundary; an application calling a third-party service is another. These boundaries help identify where validation, authentication, authorization, and monitoring are required.

## Ask what can go wrong

For each component and data flow, consider threats such as unauthorized access, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service, and privilege escalation. A blog editor, for example, may face account takeover, unauthorized publishing, malicious HTML, leaked tokens, and abuse of upload endpoints.

Do not treat a threat model as a checklist that guarantees security. Use it to prioritize realistic risks and connect each risk to a control and a test. An authentication control does not replace authorization: a signed-in user still must not be able to edit another user's content.

## Turn risks into verifiable controls

For a content-management application:
- require strong authentication for editor accounts;
- check permissions on the server for every write operation;
- validate and encode untrusted input in the correct output context;
- store secrets outside source control and rotate them if exposed;
- limit upload size and validate file type and storage location;
- rate-limit sensitive endpoints and monitor suspicious activity;
- back up important data and test restoration.

Use secure defaults and least privilege. A control should be tested, not merely documented. For example, write a test that attempts to edit a post using a different user's identifier and confirm the API denies it.

## Keep the model current

Review the model when authentication, payment flows, storage, or external integrations change. Include abuse cases and operational failures, not only malicious attacks. Keep diagrams and notes concise enough that developers will actually update them.

**Further reading:** [OWASP Threat Modeling](https://owasp.org/www-community/Threat_Modeling) and [OWASP Application Security Verification Standard](https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/).

posts.title: Cloud Run vs. Cloud Functions
posts.summary: A practical beginner-friendly guide to cloud run vs. cloud functions, with key concepts, a learning workflow, common mistakes, and next steps.
posts.body:
## The idea in plain English

Cloud Run vs. Cloud Functions is easier to understand when you connect the concept to a real problem. In software development, the goal is not to learn a tool because it is popular; it is to understand what it solves, what trade-offs it introduces, and when a simpler option is enough.

This guide introduces the core idea, the vocabulary you will encounter, and a practical way to begin. Treat the examples as learning patterns and check the official documentation for version-specific behavior before using them in production.

## Why it matters

Developers work with systems made of smaller components. A clear mental model helps you decide where a component belongs, how it communicates with the rest of the application, and how to debug it when something fails. It also helps you explain your design choices during code reviews and interviews.

For a beginner, focus on three questions:

- **Problem:** What pain point does this approach address?
- **Mechanism:** What happens step by step when it runs?
- **Trade-off:** What extra complexity, cost, or maintenance does it add?

## A practical learning workflow

1. Start with a tiny example that demonstrates one concept.
2. Run it locally and observe the output rather than copying code blindly.
3. Change one input or configuration value and predict what will happen.
4. Add error handling and test an invalid input.
5. Write down what you learned and the limits of the example.

For example, when exploring cloud run vs. cloud functions, create a small project with one responsibility. Keep configuration explicit, use meaningful names, and add a short README explaining how to run it. Small experiments make errors easier to understand than a large project assembled all at once.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Choosing a tool before defining the problem.
- Copying snippets without checking their assumptions or version.
- Ignoring security, performance, accessibility, or failure cases.
- Treating a tutorial as proof that a solution is production-ready.
- Skipping documentation and tests.

## What to learn next

After you understand the basics, build a small end-to-end project and document the decisions you made. Compare at least one alternative, test edge cases, and consult the official documentation for the framework or platform you use. That process builds durable skill—not just familiarity with terminology.

## Further reading

Start with the official documentation for the relevant language, framework, or platform. Prefer primary documentation and maintained standards over undated social posts. This article is an evergreen learning guide, not a report of a newly announced product release.

*Written for the B Tecky developer-learning community.*

Some events may explicitly include goodies in the ticket, while others may have different arrangements.

That's why the official event page for your city should always be your first source of information.

💰 Is DevFest Free?

This is another common question.

The answer is:

It depends on the event.

Google's official DevFest FAQ says that ticket prices vary by location because DevFest events are independently organized by local GDGs.

Some events are free, while others charge a fee to cover expenses such as venue and catering.

So:

Free DevFest ≠ Guaranteed free swag

and

Paid DevFest ≠ Automatically better swag.

Always look at what your particular event ticket actually includes.

📝 How to Find Your DevFest

The easiest way to start is through the official Google DevFest page.

You can find the 2026 DevFest season and look for an event near you.

🔗 Official Google DevFest Page

Google DevFest 2026 — Official Page

Google's official page says registrations open in advance and recommends registering early because some events can fill up quickly.

🎟️ A to Z: How to Attend DevFest 2026

Here's a simple process if you're attending DevFest for the first time.

Step 1 — Find Your City

Search for the DevFest event organized by the GDG community in your city.

Step 2 — Read the Event Page

Don't just look at the event poster.

Check:

Date
Venue
Ticket price
Registration requirements
Ticket benefits
Swag information
Schedule
Terms and conditions
Step 3 — Register

If tickets are available, complete the registration process.

Step 4 — Check Your Ticket Benefits

This is particularly important if you're attending mainly for swag.

Look for words such as:

“Goodies included”

“Swag included”

“Goodie kit”

or specific descriptions of what attendees receive.

Step 5 — Attend the Event

Arrive according to the event's instructions and complete the check-in process.

Step 6 — Collect Your Badge/Kit

If your event includes swag or goodies, follow the organizer's instructions for collection.

Remember: availability and distribution can vary by event.

🎓 Do Students Get Different Swag?

Sometimes.

Some events have separate Student and Professional tickets, and the benefits can differ.

For example, DevFest Hyderabad lists separate Student and Professional ticket categories and also mentions a professional-specific goodie.

So don't assume that:

Student ticket = Professional ticket = identical swag

Check your particular event.

🔥 What Else Do You Get Besides Swag?

Honestly, swag is only one part of DevFest.

The official Google DevFest page highlights things such as:

🤖 AI

Learn about modern AI technologies and how developers are using them.

☁️ Cloud

Explore Google Cloud technologies and real-world applications.

🛠️ Hands-On Learning

Participate in workshops and practical sessions.

🎤 Technical Sessions

Learn from developers, Google Developer Experts and other technology professionals.

🤝 Networking

Meet students, developers, founders, designers and other technology enthusiasts.

💡 Community

Become part of your local developer ecosystem.

Google describes DevFest as a place for technical content, community connections and hands-on learning.

📸 Should You Attend Only for Swag?

If you're going only because of a T-shirt or backpack, make sure you understand the event's actual swag policy first.

But if you're interested in AI, Cloud, Android, Web, software development or technology communities, DevFest can offer much more than merchandise.

You can potentially leave with:

Knowledge + Connections + New Ideas + Projects + Community Experience + Swag

And those first four can be much more valuable for your career than the physical goodies.

🚨 Important: Don't Fall for Fake Swag Claims

As DevFest becomes more popular, you may see posts claiming:

“Register now and Google will send you FREE swag!”

Be careful.

Don't enter personal information into random websites simply because someone promises a Google T-shirt or backpack.

Always verify:

Is the event listed through an official GDG/Google community channel?
Is the registration page legitimate?
Does the event page actually mention swag?
Are the ticket benefits clearly stated?
Is the event organized by a recognized GDG community?

When in doubt, start from the official DevFest page and navigate to the relevant event.

🎁 So, Will EVERYONE Get FREE Swags at DevFest 2026?
The simple answer:

No universal guarantee exists for every DevFest event.

Some 2026 events explicitly include goodies or swag with their tickets, while the exact benefits vary by event.

So before registering, check your city's official DevFest page and read exactly what your ticket includes.

Don't rely only on a thumbnail, Instagram post, YouTube video or someone else's swag photo.

🔗 Important Links
🌐 Google DevFest 2026

Official Google DevFest Page

📅 Find Your Local GDG Events

Google Developer Groups Events

🚀 Final Thoughts

Google DevFest 2026 is much more than a swag event.

From October 1 to December 31, developers, students, AI builders and technology enthusiasts will be gathering through community-led DevFest events around the world.

And yes, many DevFest events do offer goodies or swag, but the exact items and eligibility can vary significantly from one event to another.

So before you register, remember the golden rule:

If your event confirms swag, register early, attend the event, participate in the sessions, meet other developers, learn something new and enjoy the community experience.

And if you get a cool DevFest T-shirt or backpack along the way… that's a nice bonus. 😄🎁

posts.title: Web Accessibility Basics: Keyboard, Contrast, and Semantics
posts.summary: Make a website easier to use with semantic HTML, visible focus, clear labels, and sufficient contrast.
posts.body:
Make a website easier to use with semantic HTML, visible focus, clear labels, and sufficient contrast.

## The core idea

Accessibility improves the experience for people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification, or different input methods. Semantic HTML gives controls meaningful behavior and structure without requiring custom JavaScript for everything.

## A practical way to approach it

Use real buttons for actions and links for navigation, label form controls, maintain a logical heading order, provide visible focus styles, and test keyboard navigation. Check contrast and write useful alternative text for informative images.

## Try it in a small project

Navigate your site without a mouse. Try the search form, menu, editor, and modal dialogs using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Escape. Fix the first confusing focus jump you encounter.

## Common mistakes to avoid

Automated checkers catch only part of the problem. Test real tasks with keyboard-only navigation and do not use color as the only signal.

## Key takeaway

Keep the first version small, make your assumptions explicit, and verify the result with a repeatable test. For production use, check the current official documentation for the tools and versions you choose.

---
## Start with semantic HTML

Semantic HTML gives browsers and assistive technologies information about what page elements mean. Use headings to describe the page structure, buttons for actions, links for navigation, labels for form controls, and landmarks such as `header`, `nav`, `main`, and `footer`. A clickable `div` does not automatically behave like a button for keyboard users.

Keep heading levels meaningful and provide a descriptive page title. Form fields should have visible labels, and errors should identify the field and explain how to correct the problem. Placeholder text is not a replacement for a label because it disappears when the user types.

## Make keyboard interaction predictable

Every interactive control should be reachable and usable with a keyboard. Tab and Shift+Tab should move focus in a logical order; Enter or Space should activate controls according to their native behaviour. Focus indicators must remain visible. Avoid keyboard traps in dialogs and menus, and provide a way to close overlays with Escape when appropriate.

Test the site without a mouse. Try navigation, search, forms, accordions, dialogs, and any calculator or interactive tool. Check that focus is not hidden behind sticky headers and that the page does not unexpectedly move focus after an action.

## Check contrast and non-colour cues

Text and controls need sufficient contrast against their backgrounds. Do not communicate success, errors, or required fields using colour alone; add text, icons with accessible names, or another clear cue. Support zoom and responsive layouts so content remains usable at enlarged text sizes.

Images need alternative text when they convey information. Decorative images should not create noise for screen-reader users. The alternative text should describe the image's purpose in context, not repeat a filename.

## Use automated tools and human testing

Automated accessibility checkers can identify some missing labels, contrast problems, and structural issues, but they cannot determine whether instructions make sense or whether a workflow is understandable. Combine automated scans with keyboard testing and, where possible, screen-reader testing.

Use the WCAG success criteria as a reference and prioritize barriers that prevent users from completing important tasks. Accessibility is an ongoing quality practice, not a one-time badge.

**Further reading:** [W3C: Introduction to Web Accessibility](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/) and [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/).

posts.title: Terraform and Infrastructure as Code
posts.summary: A practical beginner-friendly guide to terraform and infrastructure as code, with key concepts, a learning workflow, common mistakes, and next steps.
posts.body:
## The idea in plain English

Terraform and Infrastructure as Code is easier to understand when you connect the concept to a real problem. In software development, the goal is not to learn a tool because it is popular; it is to understand what it solves, what trade-offs it introduces, and when a simpler option is enough.

This guide introduces the core idea, the vocabulary you will encounter, and a practical way to begin. Treat the examples as learning patterns and check the official documentation for version-specific behavior before using them in production.

## Why it matters

Developers work with systems made of smaller components. A clear mental model helps you decide where a component belongs, how it communicates with the rest of the application, and how to debug it when something fails. It also helps you explain your design choices during code reviews and interviews.

For a beginner, focus on three questions:

- **Problem:** What pain point does this approach address?
- **Mechanism:** What happens step by step when it runs?
- **Trade-off:** What extra complexity, cost, or maintenance does it add?

## A practical learning workflow

1. Start with a tiny example that demonstrates one concept.
2. Run it locally and observe the output rather than copying code blindly.
3. Change one input or configuration value and predict what will happen.
4. Add error handling and test an invalid input.
5. Write down what you learned and the limits of the example.

For example, when exploring terraform and infrastructure as code, create a small project with one responsibility. Keep configuration explicit, use meaningful names, and add a short README explaining how to run it. Small experiments make errors easier to understand than a large project assembled all at once.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Choosing a tool before defining the problem.
- Copying snippets without checking their assumptions or version.
- Ignoring security, performance, accessibility, or failure cases.
- Treating a tutorial as proof that a solution is production-ready.
- Skipping documentation and tests.

## What to learn next

After you understand the basics, build a small end-to-end project and document the decisions you made. Compare at least one alternative, test edge cases, and consult the official documentation for the framework or platform you use. That process builds durable skill—not just familiarity with terminology.

## Further reading

Start with the official documentation for the relevant language, framework, or platform. Prefer primary documentation and maintained standards over undated social posts. This article is an evergreen learning guide, not a report of a newly announced product release.

*Written for the B Tecky developer-learning community.*

posts.title: Hacktoberfest 2026: Complete 0 to HERO Guide | FREE Swags & Goodies
posts.summary: If you are a student, developer, beginner, open-source enthusiast, or someone interested in AI and software development, then Hacktoberfest 2026 is something you should know about.  Hacktoberfest is a free, month-long celebration of open source that takes place throughout October. But there is a big change in 2026: thi
posts.body:
What Is Hacktoberfest 2026?

Hacktoberfest brings developers and technology communities together to learn, build, experiment and connect around open source.

In previous years, Hacktoberfest was strongly associated with contributing to GitHub repositories and completing pull requests.

However, Hacktoberfest 2026 works differently.

Pull requests and merge requests no longer count toward Hacktoberfest rewards. The organizers have changed the format to reduce low-effort or spam contributions and instead encourage participants to learn and build with open-source AI and open-weight models.

So if you're completely new to open source, you don't need to be an expert GitHub contributor to participate this year.

🎯 What Can You Do in Hacktoberfest 2026?

There are several ways to participate.

💻 1. Online Activities

You can participate from anywhere through online Hacktoberfest activities.

These include:

Livestreams
DEV Challenges
Global Hack Week
Open-source AI activities
Community sessions
Various challenges and learning activities

The official Hacktoberfest activities page currently lists multiple ways to earn virtual stickers throughout October.

🤖 2. Build With Open-Source AI

One of the biggest themes of Hacktoberfest 2026 is open-source AI and open-weight models.

This makes the event particularly interesting if you're currently learning:

Artificial Intelligence
Machine Learning
Generative AI
LLMs
AI Agents
Python
Open-source software
Developer tools

You don't necessarily need to build a complicated AI system.

The goal is to learn, experiment and share what you build.

🏆 3. Participate in DEV Challenges

Hacktoberfest 2026 includes a Launch Weekend challenge followed by four weekly DEV Challenges.

The official schedule includes:

Launch Weekend: October 2–4
Week 1: October 5–11
Week 2: October 12–18
Week 3: October 19–25
Week 4: October 26–31

These challenges are centered around open-source AI, and participation requires a DEV account.

Some challenges may also have cash prizes, so make sure you read the individual challenge rules before submitting anything.

🎁 How Can You Get FREE Swag?

This is probably the part many people are waiting for. 😄

Hacktoberfest 2026 has changed the reward system, but participants can still earn physical rewards.

For online participation, you can collect virtual stickers by completing eligible activities.

Once you collect the required stickers, Hacktoberfest will send a physical sticker pack to eligible participants.

And there is an additional milestone:

⭐ Earn 10 Virtual Stickers

According to the official Hacktoberfest website, collecting 10 virtual stickers unlocks a bonus holographic sticker in your mailed sticker pack.

🏅 Become a Completionist

If you collect 17 stickers, you become a Hacktoberfest Completionist and are automatically entered into a raffle for a Hacktoberfest 2026 T-shirt or Arduino Uno Q board.

So there are multiple milestones to work toward instead of simply counting pull requests.

🧑‍💻 What About In-Person Hacktoberfest Events?

Hacktoberfest isn't only online.

There are 300+ Fests happening around the world, including Hack Days and community Meetups.

🔥 Hack Day

A Hack Day is basically a mini hackathon.

You can:

Build a project
Work individually or in a team
Experiment with open-source AI
Demo your project
Compete for prizes
🤝 Meetup

Meetups are more community-focused and can include:

Technical talks
Workshops
Panels
Discussions
Networking

You don't necessarily need to build a project for a Meetup.

🎒 Can You Get T-Shirts and Other Swag?

Yes, but there is an important point.

In-person Fests have T-shirts, stickers and other swag while supplies last. However, swag is not guaranteed, and distribution is determined by the individual event host.

Online participants can earn the official sticker pack through the online activity system, but T-shirts are not promised for online participation.

So don't assume that completing an online challenge automatically means you'll receive every piece of physical merchandise shown in promotional content.

📝 Hacktoberfest 2026: Step-by-Step

If you're starting from zero, here's a simple approach.

Step 1️⃣

Go to the official Hacktoberfest website and create/sign into your MyMLH account.

Step 2️⃣

Complete your participant profile and add your postal address if you want to receive the sticker pack.

Step 3️⃣

Connect your DEV account if you want to participate in the DEV Challenges.

Step 4️⃣

Check the available activities on your participant dashboard.

Step 5️⃣

Start completing activities such as livestreams, challenges, Global Hack Week activities and other eligible tasks.

Step 6️⃣

Track your virtual stickers and milestones.

Step 7️⃣

If you want the in-person experience, find a Hacktoberfest Fest near your city and register separately through its event page.

The official FAQ states that each in-person Fest has its own registration.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals: Improve Speed Without Guesswork
posts.summary: Understand LCP, INP, and CLS, measure real user experience, and work through a repeatable performance-improvement process.
posts.body:
A page can feel slow even when the server responds quickly. Large images may delay the main content, JavaScript can make controls feel unresponsive, and late-loading elements can move text just as a visitor starts reading. Core Web Vitals provide a focused way to measure three parts of user experience: loading, responsiveness, and visual stability.

This guide explains the metrics and a practical process for improving them without chasing a score that does not reflect what visitors actually experience.

## 1. The three Core Web Vitals

**Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)** measures when the largest visible content element in the viewport is rendered. It often reflects the loading of a hero image, large heading, or main content block. A useful target is 2.5 seconds or less at the 75th percentile of page visits.

**Interaction to Next Paint (INP)** measures interaction responsiveness across a page visit. It considers delays around user interactions such as clicks, taps, and keyboard input. A useful target is 200 milliseconds or less at the 75th percentile.

**Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)** measures unexpected visual movement. A useful target is 0.1 or less. Content that shifts because an image has no reserved dimensions or an advertisement is inserted without space can make a page frustrating to use.

These are field-oriented thresholds, not promises that every visit will meet the target. Evaluate the 75th percentile separately for mobile and desktop where data is available.

## 2. Measure before changing code

Start with a specific URL and a specific user task. Check whether the issue affects the homepage, an article template, a calculator, or the entire site. Use more than one source:

- PageSpeed Insights provides field data when sufficient Chrome User Experience Report data exists, plus lab diagnostics.
- Chrome DevTools Performance helps identify long tasks, rendering work, and layout shifts during a controlled test.
- Search Console's Core Web Vitals report groups URLs by field performance when data is available.
- Real-user monitoring can help teams understand how performance varies across devices, networks, and locations.

A lab test is a controlled snapshot. Field data reflects actual visits and can vary by audience and device. If a page has no field data, that does not mean it is fast; it may simply lack enough eligible traffic.

## 3. Improve LCP by prioritizing the main content

First identify the actual LCP element. If it is a large image, serve an appropriately sized image, use a modern format where supported, compress it, and avoid loading a much larger asset than the layout needs.

Do not lazy-load the image that is immediately visible and expected to become the LCP element. Lazy loading is usually more appropriate for below-the-fold images. Make sure the browser can discover critical resources early, and avoid placing important content behind a large client-side rendering step.

Also inspect server response time and render-blocking resources. A slow backend, excessive CSS, or a script that blocks rendering can delay the main content even if the image itself is optimized.

## 4. Improve INP by reducing unnecessary main-thread work

A browser's main thread handles many tasks, including JavaScript, style calculation, layout, and painting. If a click triggers a large synchronous calculation, the interface may stop responding until that work finishes.

Useful improvements include:

- Break long JavaScript tasks into smaller units and yield between them when appropriate.
- Avoid running expensive filtering or formatting work on every keystroke when a debounced or incremental approach is suitable.
- Reduce unnecessary event handlers and repeated DOM updates.
- Load non-essential scripts only when they are needed.
- Keep interaction feedback immediate, even if the full result takes longer.

Do not remove useful functionality simply to improve a metric. Profile the slow interaction first, then optimize the code path that blocks the response.

## 5. Improve CLS by reserving space

Images and video embeds should have known dimensions or an aspect ratio so the browser can reserve space before the media loads. Ad slots, banners, and dynamically inserted UI should also have predictable space.

Web fonts can cause text to reflow when the final font loads. Use sensible fallback fonts and configure font loading carefully. Avoid inserting a new banner above existing content after the visitor has started reading; if an element must appear, reserve its space or place it where it will not push the page around.

A practical test is to load the page on a slow connection and watch whether the text or controls move unexpectedly.

## 6. A repeatable optimization workflow

Use this sequence for each page template:

1. Record the URL, device type, test conditions, and baseline metrics.
2. Identify the actual LCP element, slow interaction, or layout shift source.
3. Choose one change with a clear reason.
4. Test the change locally and compare the same page under similar conditions.
5. Check that accessibility, content, and functionality still work.
6. Deploy the change and monitor field data over time.

Changing many unrelated things at once makes it hard to know what helped. Keep a short change log with the metric, suspected cause, change, and observed result.

## 7. Common mistakes

**Optimizing only for a Lighthouse score:** a score is a diagnostic signal, not the whole user experience. Field data and real task completion matter.

**Lazy-loading every image:** lazy loading the main above-the-fold image can make LCP worse. Prioritize the visible content and defer what is genuinely below the fold.

**Removing all JavaScript:** some JavaScript is essential to the task. Remove redundant work and delay non-critical code instead of breaking useful interactions.

**Ignoring mobile:** slower CPUs, smaller screens, and variable networks often expose issues that a desktop test hides.

**Assuming one test proves a fix:** performance varies. Repeat tests, compare field data when available, and avoid drawing conclusions from a single run.

## 8. A practical exercise

Choose one article page and one interactive tool page. Record mobile and desktop measurements. On the article, inspect the hero image and font loading. On the tool, profile a common interaction and identify any long task. Fix one issue on each page, then retest. Finally, check the pages on a real mobile device and confirm that the content remains stable while loading.

## Further reading

- [web.dev: Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals)
- [web.dev: Optimize Largest Contentful Paint](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp)
- [web.dev: Optimize Interaction to Next Paint](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-inp)
- [web.dev: Optimize Cumulative Layout Shift](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-cls)
- [PageSpeed Insights](https://pagespeed.web.dev/)

## Key takeaways

Measure the experience before changing code. Find the real LCP element, profile the interaction that feels slow, and reserve space for content that loads later. Improve one cause at a time, verify that the page still works, and use field data—not a single lab score—as the longer-term check.
